slides.title: The Second Law: why things only go one way

blocks.text: AME 101 · Chapter 7 · Second Law, entropy, engines and refrigerators
Lecture runs 50 minutes with 24 votes.
“What does the Earth get from the sun?”
Take two or three shouted answers (expect energy, heat, light), then run Vote 1.

slides.title: Compared with the energy Earth receives from the Sun, how much does Earth radiate back to space?

blocks.text: C. Essentially the same amount
Over time, energy in equals energy out. Otherwise Earth would keep heating up.
So if Earth gives all the energy back, what is it actually getting from the Sun? Hold that thought.

slides.title: The First Law is not the whole story

blocks.text: It says energy is conserved. It says nothing about which direction a process goes.
Methane and air at 300 K burn to CO2, H2O and N2 at 2000 K.
The reverse would conserve energy too. Nobody has ever seen it happen.
Call-on: Name an everyday process you have never seen run backward.
A property of a substance: a measure of its “disorganization” or “randomness.”
More spread out means we know less about where the molecules are, so entropy is higher.
Another way to see it: entropy tracks how spread out the energy is.
The entropy of an isolated system always increases or remains the same
Burning raises entropy, so it happens on its own.
Un-burning is possible only by raising the entropy of the surroundings by more.
Clausius, 1865: the energy of the universe is constant; its entropy tends to a maximum.
Ω (omega) is the number of different ways the system can hold its energy.
Example: 3 atoms share 2 packets of energy. Count the boxes: Ω = 6.
k = 1.38 × 10−23 J/K is Boltzmann's constant.

slides.title: A system has exactly one way to hold its energy (Ω = 1). Its entropy S = k ln(Ω) is:

blocks.text: ln(1) = 0. One arrangement means no uncertainty and no disorganization.
Example from the notes: a mass raised to a given height.

slides.title: Why do we never see a cold spoon make hot coffee hotter?
options: Atoms cannot pass energy to faster atoms
It is allowed, but overwhelmingly improbable with about 10^26 atoms

blocks.text: C. It is allowed, but overwhelmingly improbable with about 10^26 atoms
The First Law is satisfied either way.
The odds are what rule it out: there are vastly more spread-out arrangements than bunched-up ones.
No device can have as its only effect the transfer of heat from cold to hot
Otherwise an object at uniform temperature could become hot on one side and cold on the other by itself.
A refrigerator moves heat from cold to hot, but it needs a work input.

slides.title: 1,000 J of heat flows from a block at 500 K to a block at 250 K. The entropy change of the universe is:

blocks.text: D. +2 J/K
Hot block: −1000/500 = −2 J/K. Cold block: +1000/250 = +4 J/K.
Total: +2 J/K. Positive, so the process is allowed (and irreversible).

slides.title: You can’t win; you can’t break even

blocks.text: First Law: put 1 J of heat in, and you cannot get more than 1 J of work out. “You can’t win.”
Second Law: you cannot even get the full 1 J of work out. “You can’t break even.”
η ≤ 1 − TL/TH
It depends only on the two temperatures, not on the design or the materials.
Hotter source or colder sink: higher limit.

slides.title: An inventor claims an engine that takes in 100 J of heat at 600 K, rejects heat at 300 K, and delivers 70 J of work. This engine:

blocks.text: B. Violates the Second Law only
Energy balances: 30 J is rejected.
But the Carnot limit is 1 − 300/600 = 50%. A claim of 70% breaks the Second Law.

slides.title: A steam engine runs between 160 °C steam and 22 °C surroundings. Its best possible efficiency is about:

blocks.text: 1 − 295/433 = 0.32. Use kelvin: 86% is what you get with °C.
Real engines of Carnot’s day managed about 3%.
The entropy of an isolated system never decreases. S = k ln(Ω).
Heat goes from hot to cold unless you pay with work. ΔS ≥ Q/T.
Engines: η ≤ 1 − TL/TH.
Refrigerator: COP < TL/(TH − TL). Heat pump: COP < TH/(TH − TL).

slides.title: Which statement agrees with the Second Law?
options: Heat can never go from cold to hot
The entropy of any object can never decrease
Energy gets used up over time
The entropy of an isolated system never decreases; a local decrease is paid for elsewhere

blocks.text: D. The entropy of an isolated system never decreases; a local decrease is paid for elsewhere
A is false once you add work. B ignores the surroundings. C contradicts the First Law.
D is the Second Law.
Earth is not a closed system.
The Sun supplies concentrated, low-entropy energy. Earth sends the same amount of energy back, spread out.
About 20 low-energy photons leave for every solar photon that arrives.
